Each op is a tuple `(start, end, color)` with integer `start` and `end` and a string `color`, and it paints the half-open range `[start, end)` of a number line. Apply the ops in list order to an initially blank line, each op overwriting whatever earlier ops put in its range, and return the final painting as a list of `(start, end, color)` tuples sorted by `start`, covering only the painted parts of the line.

An op with `start == end` paints nothing, and neither does an op with `start > end`; just skip those. Also, a color of `None` means erase: that op's range becomes blank again, and blank parts never appear in the output.

The output pieces have to be maximal runs. If two pieces touch (one's `end` equals the other's `start`) and have the same color, report them as one tuple, no matter which ops produced them: painting `(0, 3, 'red')` and then `(3, 6, 'red')` gives `[(0, 6, 'red')]`, not two tuples.

Add underpainting: if an op's color string starts with `'^'`, it only paints the parts of its range that are blank at that moment, using the color without the leading `'^'`; parts that are already painted keep their current color.

turns.text: Write `def run_jobs(jobs: list) -> list` simulating one machine that runs one job at a time, each to completion without interruption. Each job is a tuple `(name, arrival, duration, priority)` with integer times and priority, unique names and positive durations; whenever the machine is free, it runs the waiting job with the highest priority. Return a list of `(name, start, end)` tuples in the order the jobs run.

The machine starts at time 0. A job can only be picked once it has arrived (arrival <= current time), and a job that arrives exactly when the machine becomes free is eligible for that pick. If no job is waiting, the machine stays idle until the next arrival.

Two more rules for the pick. When priorities tie, take the earliest arrival, then the name alphabetically. And add aging: instead of comparing raw priorities, at each pick every waiting job's priority is boosted by 1 for every full 5 time units it has waited so far, i.e. by `(current_time - arrival) // 5`. The boosted priority is what gets compared; ties still fall back to earliest arrival, then name.

I think there's a compounding bug in the aging: each time the machine picks a job, the jobs still waiting get a new boost added on top of the boost they already received at the previous pick, instead of the boost being recomputed from their original priority. Please fix that.

reference:
def run_jobs(jobs):
    pending = list(jobs)
    t = 0
    out = []
    while pending:
        ready = [j for j in pending if j[1] <= t]
        if not ready:
            t = min(j[1] for j in pending)
            continue
        best = min(ready, key=lambda j: (-(j[3] + (t - j[1]) // 5), j[1], j[0]))
        pending.remove(best)
        out.append((best[0], t, t + best[2]))
        t += best[2]
    return out

turns.text: Write `def reachable(grid: list, start: tuple) -> int`. `grid` is a list of equal-length strings where each character is a digit `'0'`-`'9'` giving that cell's height, or `'#'` for a wall; `start` is a `(row, col)` pair and is never a wall. Moving up, down, left or right, return how many distinct cells can be reached from `start`, counting `start` itself.
Heights limit movement: you can step onto a neighbouring cell only if it is inside the grid, not a wall, and at most 1 higher than the cell you are on. Stepping down by any amount is fine.

Add ice: the character `'='` is an ice cell with height 0. Stepping onto ice follows the normal height rule, but then you slide: you keep moving in the same direction for as long as the next cell in that direction is inside the grid and is also ice, and you stop on the last ice cell. If `start` is ice you begin standing on it without sliding, and from any ice cell you are standing on you can step in any direction as usual.

To be clear about what counts as reached on ice: only cells you can stop on count. Ice cells you merely slide across without stopping are not reached and must not be counted, unless you can stop on them some other way.

Make the step limits configurable: the signature becomes `def reachable(grid: list, start: tuple, max_climb: int = 1, max_drop: int = None) -> int`. A step may go up by at most `max_climb` and down by at most `max_drop` (`None` means any drop is allowed, as before). These limits apply to every step onto a cell, including stepping onto ice; sliding from ice to ice never changes height, so it is never blocked by them.

def test_climb_rule_is_asymmetric():
    grid = ["013",
            "0#2",
            "000"]
    assert reachable(grid, (0, 0)) == 6
    assert reachable(grid, (0, 2)) == 8

def test_walls_isolate():
    assert reachable(["0#", "#0"], (0, 0)) == 1
    assert reachable(["5"], (0, 0)) == 1

def test_ice_slide_stops_on_last_ice():
    assert reachable(["0===1"], (0, 0)) == 4

def test_ice_maze_counts_only_stopping_cells():
    grid = ["1==#",
            "0=9=",
            "2==="]
    assert reachable(grid, (0, 0)) == 8

def test_start_on_ice():
    assert reachable(["===", "#0#"], (0, 1)) == 4

def test_configurable_climb():
    grid = ["0246",
            "1357",
            "#9#8"]
    assert reachable(grid, (0, 0)) == 2
    assert reachable(grid, (0, 0), max_climb=2) == 9

def test_drop_limit_applies_when_stepping_onto_ice():
    assert reachable(["5=0"], (0, 0)) == 3
    assert reachable(["5=0"], (0, 0), max_drop=1) == 1
    assert reachable(["30", "1="], (0, 0), max_drop=2) == 4

def test_limits_combined_with_ice():
    grid = ["2==0",
            "3#=1",

    assert reachable(grid, (0, 0), max_climb=1, max_drop=1) == 3

Within a group, names with equal scores are ordered alphabetically, and a group with `k` or fewer names keeps them all. Also, a name may appear more than once in the same group; treat it as a single name with its highest score in that group (the same name in different groups is unrelated).

Don't split ties at the cutoff. Keep the first `k` names in that order, plus every further name whose score equals the score of the `k`-th kept name, so a group can end up with more than `k` names. For example, with scores x=8, y=6, z=6, w=2 and `k=2`, the group keeps `['x', 'y', 'z']`.
One edge case: if `k` is 0 or negative, return an empty dict, not a dict of groups with empty lists.

Scores can now be `None`, meaning the name took part but has no score. Unscored names rank after all scored names (alphabetically among themselves), count toward `k` like any other name, and are tied with each other, so if the `k`-th kept name is unscored, every unscored name in the group is kept. If a name has both scored and `None` rows in a group, use its highest real score.

notes: v0.3 5-turn shard (2026-10-30); final spec equivalent to old t1+t2+t3. Shards: T1 plain top-k per group; T2 alphabetical ties, small groups, duplicate names keep max; T3 tie-inclusive cutoff (overturns strict top-k); T4 k<=0 -> {} (overturns {g: []}); T5 None scores last, tied together, never override a real score. Old notes: Top-k with tie-inclusive cutoff by k-th position (not k-th distinct score); T2 breaks name uniqueness, T3 adds None that must sort last, tie only with None, and never override a real score. Mutants: no dedupe, first score kept, strict top-k, None as 0, None overrides, cross-group merge.

turns.text: Write `def sessionize(events: list, timeout: int) -> list`. Each event is a tuple `(user, timestamp)` with an integer timestamp. Split each user's events, taken in time order, into sessions, using `timeout` as the inactivity cutoff between consecutive events, and return a list of `(user, start, end, count)` tuples, one per session, where `start` and `end` are the first and last timestamps in the session and `count` is how many events it contains.
The events list is in no particular order, and a user can have several events at the same timestamp; they are separate events and all of them count toward `count`.

Sessions now also have a maximum length: the signature becomes `def sessionize(events: list, timeout: int, max_len: int) -> list`, and an event also starts a new session if it comes more than `max_len` units after the first event of the current session.

Two clarifications. On the cutoff: an event exactly `timeout` units after that user's previous event stays in the same session; only a gap of more than `timeout` starts a new one. And don't group the result by user: sort the whole list by `start`, then by `user`.

Events may now carry a kind: an event is either `(user, timestamp)` or `(user, timestamp, kind)`. An event whose kind is `'logout'` joins whichever session the usual rules put it in, and then closes that session, so the user's next event always starts a new one. Other kinds behave like plain events. When a user has a logout and other events at the same timestamp, the logout comes after them.

notes: v0.3 5-turn shard (2026-10-30); final spec equivalent to old t1+t2+t3. Shards: T1 gap sessionisation (boundary and output order unstated); T2 unordered/same-timestamp events; T3 max_len from session start; T4 exact-timeout stays + sort by (start, user) instead of grouping by user (overturn); T5 logout kind with same-timestamp ordering. Old notes: Per-user gap sessionisation with two split rules (gap from previous event vs span from session start) plus a T3 closing event with same-timestamp ordering and mixed tuple arity. Mutants: >= timeout, max_len from previous, logout excluded, sort by user, logout first at a tie, duplicates collapsed.

turns.text: Write `def make_change(amount: int, drawer: dict) -> dict`. `drawer` maps a coin value (a positive int) to how many coins of that value are available. Pay out exactly `amount` greedily, going through the coin values from largest to smallest and taking as many coins of each value as possible without going over the remaining amount or the available count, and return a dict mapping each coin value used to the number of coins used (values that aren't used are left out).
If the amount can't be paid exactly, return `None`. An `amount` of 0 returns `{}`.

Drop the greedy rule. Instead, return the way of paying exactly `amount`, within the available counts, that uses the fewest coins in total, and return `None` only if no exact payment exists at all. For example, paying 12 from plenty of 9s, 6s and 1s should give two 6s, not a 9 and three 1s.
When several ways tie on the number of coins, prefer the one using more coins of the largest value; if still tied, more of the next largest value, and so on.

The drawer must never be emptied: at least one coin of every value has to stay in it, so at most `count - 1` coins of a value can be used, and a value with a count of 1 or less can't be used at all (counts can be 0 or even negative because of data-entry mistakes).

notes: v0.3 5-turn shard (2026-10-30); final spec equivalent to old t1+t2+t3. Shards: T1 greedy change; T2 None on failure, 0 -> {}; T3 replaces greedy with fewest coins (explicit overturn); T4 lexicographic larger-coin tie-break; T5 keep-one-coin reserve with bad-count clamping. Old notes: T2 replaces greedy with bounded fewest-coins search plus a lexicographic tie-break; T3 shrinks every count and must clamp bad counts. Mutants: greedy, reversed tie-break, no reserve, single coin usable, negative counts unclamped, zero entries reported.

turns.text: Write `def best_route(edges: list, start: str, goal: str) -> tuple`. Each edge is a tuple `(a, b, cost)` connecting two named nodes with a non-negative integer cost. Find the cheapest route from `start` to `goal` and return `(total_cost, nodes)`, where `nodes` is the list of node names along the route from `start` to `goal`.
Edges can be travelled in both directions, and there can be several edges between the same two nodes. If `start == goal`, return `(0, [start])`, and if `goal` can't be reached, return `None`.

Ties matter here. Among equally cheap routes, choose the one with the fewest edges; if that still ties, choose the route whose list of node names is smallest when compared element by element as strings.
Some edges are one-way after all: an edge may have a fourth element `'oneway'`, which means it can only be travelled from `a` to `b`. Edges with three elements are still two-way.

Add a hop limit: the signature becomes `def best_route(edges: list, start: str, goal: str, max_edges: int = None) -> tuple`. When `max_edges` is given, only routes using at most that many edges are allowed, and the same preferences pick among them; return `None` if no allowed route exists. `max_edges=None` means no limit.

tests:
def test_cheapest_route():
    assert best_route([('A', 'B', 1), ('B', 'C', 1), ('A', 'C', 3)], 'A', 'C') == (2, ['A', 'B', 'C'])

def test_fewest_edges_breaks_cost_tie():
    assert best_route([('A', 'B', 1), ('B', 'C', 1), ('A', 'C', 2)], 'A', 'C') == (2, ['A', 'C'])
    assert best_route([('A', 'B', 0), ('B', 'C', 0), ('A', 'C', 0)], 'A', 'C') == (0, ['A', 'C'])

def test_name_order_breaks_remaining_ties():
    edges = [('S', 'b', 1), ('b', 'T', 1), ('S', 'a', 1), ('a', 'T', 1)]
    assert best_route(edges, 'S', 'T') == (2, ['S', 'a', 'T'])
    assert best_route([('A', 'B', 5), ('B', 'A', 2)], 'A', 'B') == (2, ['A', 'B'])

def test_one_way_edges():
    edges = [('A', 'B', 1, 'oneway'), ('B', 'C', 1), ('C', 'A', 10)]
    assert best_route(edges, 'A', 'C') == (2, ['A', 'B', 'C'])
    assert best_route(edges, 'C', 'A') == (10, ['C', 'A'])
    assert best_route(edges, 'B', 'A') == (11, ['B', 'C', 'A'])

def test_unreachable_and_trivial():
    assert best_route([('A', 'B', 1, 'oneway')], 'B', 'A') is None
    assert best_route([('A', 'B', 1)], 'A', 'Z') is None
    assert best_route([], 'X', 'X') == (0, ['X'])

def test_hop_limit():
    edges = [('A', 'B', 1), ('B', 'C', 1), ('C', 'D', 1), ('A', 'D', 10), ('A', 'E', 2), ('E', 'D', 2)]
    assert best_route(edges, 'A', 'D') == (3, ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D'])
    assert best_route(edges, 'A', 'D', max_edges=2) == (4, ['A', 'E', 'D'])
    assert best_route(edges, 'A', 'D', max_edges=1) == (10, ['A', 'D'])
    assert best_route(edges, 'A', 'D', max_edges=0) is None

def test_hop_limit_needs_more_expensive_prefix():
    edges = [('A', 'p', 1), ('p', 'X', 1), ('A', 'X', 5), ('X', 'G', 1)]
    assert best_route(edges, 'A', 'G') == (3, ['A', 'p', 'X', 'G'])
    assert best_route(edges, 'A', 'G', max_edges=2) == (6, ['A', 'X', 'G'])
notes: v0.3 5-turn shard (2026-10-30); final spec equivalent to old t1+t2+t3. Shards: T1 cheapest route; T2 two-way multi-edges, trivial/unreachable cases; T3 fewest-edges then node-list tie-break (overturns discovery-order ties); T4 'oneway' edges (overturns all-two-way); T5 max_edges hop limit. Old notes: Shortest path with a three-level tie-break (cost, edges, node-name list); T3's hop limit silently breaks node-visited Dijkstra, which needs (node, hops) states. Mutants: node-visited Dijkstra, one-way ignored/reversed, name before edge count, discovery-order ties.

turns.text: Write `def common_free(busy: dict, day_start: int, day_end: int, min_len: int) -> list`. `busy` maps each person's name to a list of `(start, end)` busy intervals in minutes. Find the times within the day when nobody is busy and return them as a list of `(start, end)` tuples sorted by start, leaving out free stretches shorter than `min_len` minutes.

All intervals are half-open `[start, end)`, and so are the day `[day_start, day_end)` and every tuple you return. A person's intervals are in no particular order and may overlap each other, a person may have no intervals at all, and busy intervals can extend beyond the day; only the part inside the day matters. Each returned tuple must be a maximal free stretch, never split into pieces.

Add a buffer around meetings: the signature becomes `def common_free(busy: dict, day_start: int, day_end: int, min_len: int, buffer: int) -> list`, and every busy interval is widened by `buffer` minutes on each side (to `[start - buffer, end + buffer)`) before anything else is done. That includes restricting it to the day: widen first, then cut to the day, so a meeting that ends shortly before the day starts can still block the start of the day once widened. The day boundaries themselves get no buffer.

I think the buffer is being double-counted between meetings. For example, with `buffer=10`, busy intervals `[60, 90)` and `[130, 160)` and a day of `[0, 300)`, the free gap between them should be `[100, 120)`, but I believe your code subtracts the buffer from that gap twice, so it comes out shorter. Please fix it.

I ran it again with `buffer=10`, busy intervals `[60, 90)` and `[130, 160)` and a day of `[0, 300)`, and the gap between them still comes out shorter than `[100, 120)` because the buffer is taken off it twice. Please actually fix the double-counting this time.

notes: v0.3 5-turn shard (2026-10-30); final spec equivalent to old t1+t2. Shards: T1 common free time; T2 half-open, overlap, clipping, maximal stretches; T3 buffer widened BEFORE clipping to the day (overturns clip-then-process order from T2), no buffer on day edges. pb1 = old T3 claim; pb2 repeats the same checkable example, false for correct T3 code.
